strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: systematic evaluation of multilingual chart understanding in LVLMs
Clever decoupled pipeline design (JSON data + Plotly code) enabling scalable multilingual expansion
Substantial benchmark scale (22,606 charts, 26,151 QA pairs across 10 languages) with balanced chart type coverage
Rigorous multi-stage quality control including back-translation consistency checks and human validation with high agreement (91-94%)
Comprehensive empirical evaluation of 16 state-of-the-art models providing clear baselines and identifying significant gaps
Excellent transparency through full prompt templates in appendix and detailed dataset statistics
Clear demonstration that current models substantially underperform on non-English languages, especially low-resource languages with non-Latin scripts
weaknesses: Limited language coverage (only 10 languages despite 65% population claim); missing major regions (Africa, Southeast Asia, etc.)
Systemic dependency on Gemini 2.5 Pro translation with no analysis of whether translation quality varies across language pairs or script types
Shallow error analysis: no detailed investigation of why models fail on specific languages/chart types/scripts despite identifying gaps
Methodological concerns: single-run results without confidence intervals or significance testing contradict benchmarking best practices
Cross-lingual transfer analysis (Table 4) shows expected findings without deep exploration; few-shot regressions noted but not explained
Dataset inherits biases from English seed corpora (ChartQA, ChartX); 17-20% data cleaning lacks detailed impact analysis
Limited qualitative examples of failure modes beyond motivating Figure 1; findings (models fail on low-resource languages) lack novelty or actionable insights
No human performance baseline provided; unclear what constitutes 'good' performance; human evaluation limited to English-Chinese subset only

strengths: Addresses a genuine gap in multilingual chart understanding benchmarks with coverage of 10 typologically diverse languages representing 65% of global population
Thoughtful decoupled data pipeline separating chart data (JSON) from rendering code (Plotly) enables reproducible, scalable multilingual chart generation
Rigorous multi-stage quality control combining automated consistency checks and human evaluation with >90% agreement between human and model-based assessments
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 16 LVLMs (open-source general, open-source multilingual, closed-source) with multiple evaluation settings (zero-shot, few-shot, cross-lingual)
Extensive documentation and transparency with detailed prompt templates, per-language statistics, and evaluation methodologies supporting reproducibility
Clear motivation for the work with concrete demonstration (Figure 1) of inconsistent cross-lingual model behavior
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the contribution is primarily a dataset resource with standard quality control practices rather than research innovation; JSON+code decoupling and LLM-based translation are conventional approaches

Critical validation gap: human evaluation restricted to single language pair (English-Chinese with 250 samples); claim that Gemini simulates human evaluation is unverified for other languages, particularly low-resource languages like Bengali and Urdu

Translation quality concerns: heavy reliance on Gemini 2.5 Pro as sole translation model introduces unknown language-specific biases; METEOR threshold of 0.6 lacks justification; no human validation of translation for 8 of 10 target languages

Insufficient depth of analysis: main finding (English > high-resource > low-resource) is unsurprising; no error categorization or systematic investigation of failure modes; no explanation for why specialized multilingual models (PALO, Centurio) severely underperform general models

Lack of statistical rigor: single-run evaluations with no confidence intervals or significance testing; no inter-annotator agreement metrics beyond exact match (missing Cohen's κ or Fleiss' κ); prompt engineering effects not explored

Limited human validation scope for a multilingual resource: inter-annotator agreement only reported as exact match percentages without formal kappa scores; disagreement resolution process minimally described; no human evaluation across all language pairs

Dataset construction biases: only 2 seed English sources (ChartQA, ChartX) without analysis of inherited biases; 17-20% data deletion without residual bias analysis; charts from existing sources may not represent real-world multilingual chart usage; translation-derived methodology may introduce artifacts not present in native multilingual data

Missing critical investigations: no per-chart-type performance breakdown; no analysis of which question types fail systematically; few-shot results (Table 3) show mixed/regressing performance without explanation; cross-lingual analysis (Table 4) limited to 4 models; no ablation studies isolating sources of performance gaps

strengths: Addresses important gap: first large-scale multilingual benchmark for chart question answering covering 10 languages and 65% of global population
Well-designed decoupled pipeline separating chart data (JSON) from rendering code, enabling flexible multilingual generation and future extensibility

Rigorous multi-stage quality control including code validation, visual fidelity checks, dual model validation (Gemini + GPT-4.1), back-translation consistency (METEOR > 0.6), and human evaluation confirming >90% quality
Large-scale dataset with 22,606 charts, 26,151 QA pairs across 16 chart types, providing diverse and balanced multilingual resource
Comprehensive systematic evaluation of 18 state-of-the-art models with zero-shot, few-shot, and cross-lingual settings, revealing significant language-specific performance gaps
Clear demonstration that native (fully localized) language settings substantially outperform mixed-language configurations, providing actionable insight
Excellent reproducibility: detailed methodology, comprehensive prompts in appendix, explicit limitations, and commitment to release dataset
weaknesses: Limited task scope: benchmark covers only question answering, excluding chart summarization, chart-to-table conversion, and other chart understanding tasks that would provide broader assessment
Multilingual data constructed through translation of English charts/QAs rather than independent creation, potentially missing language-specific chart comprehension challenges and cultural conventions
Statistical rigor concerns: all results from single runs without confidence intervals, error bars, or significance testing, limiting assessment of result stability despite deterministic inference

Limited analytical depth on failure modes: few-shot results show unexplained variance; poor performance of multilingual-specialized models lacks investigation; missing error analysis on specific language/script failures
Human evaluation restricted to English-Chinese subset (N=250) with Gemini proxy used for other languages; validation across more language pairs would strengthen claims about quality

Surprisingly low absolute performance across the board (best model 68.5%, most open-source <50%), raising questions about task difficulty, answer normalization methodology, or evaluation appropriateness
Seed data selection criteria somewhat arbitrary: exclusion of DVQA/PlotQA/ChartQA-Pro/ChartXiv justified primarily by practical complexity reasons; METEOR threshold of 0.6 lacks justification
Limited language coverage: only 10 languages, leaving significant gaps in low-resource languages outside major language families despite covering 65% of population

strengths: Addresses important gap: First large-scale multilingual chart QA benchmark filling a clear need for more inclusive evaluation of LVLMs across diverse languages
Rigorous data curation: Multi-stage quality control with automated validation, human verification (κ̄w > 0.8), and detailed filtering statistics demonstrating careful engineering

Comprehensive evaluation: 22 representative models systematically evaluated with zero-shot analysis, cross-lingual studies, fine-tuning results across architectures, and multi-dimensional error analysis
Strong reproducibility: All prompts in appendices, detailed pipeline descriptions, source licenses documented, human evaluation setup fully specified, enabling reproduction and future extensions
Substantial resource: 22.6K test charts + 26.1K QA pairs across 10 languages spanning 16 chart types, plus 751K training QA pairs—likely to be valuable benchmark for community
Practical utility demonstrated: Fine-tuning on training set yields consistent 20-90% improvements across diverse model families and sizes, showing genuine utility
Clear insights into LVLM limitations: Identifies OCR failure (27.8-51.4%) and language bias (26.8-61.5%) as dominant error sources, documents performance degradation for low-resource languages
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Pipeline employs standard techniques (extract→translate→render) without novel methodological contributions; primarily engineering work leveraging existing tools (Gemini, Plotly)

Insufficient validation of LLM-dependent quality: Heavy reliance on Gemini-2.5-Pro for extraction, translation, and quality checking without comparison to alternatives; back-translation may propagate rather than detect errors; no ablation on QC impact

Shallow analysis of failure mechanisms: Error analysis identifies categories but not root causes; no investigation of tokenization effects, language model vs. vision encoder contributions, or linguistic feature analysis explaining why models fail

Incomplete language representation: Only 4/10 languages identified as low-resource; excludes many underrepresented languages despite inclusivity framing; content biases from English sources not analyzed or addressed

Incomplete cross-lingual analysis: Table 4 covers only 4 models; no linguistic feature analysis identifying which properties (morphology, script, syntax) drive gaps; fine-tuning ablations disconnected from main narrative

Limited human evaluation scope: Only 20% of test set evaluated; conflict resolution procedure for annotators unspecified; annotator qualification criteria somewhat vague; no analysis of disagreement patterns

Metric limitations unaddressed: Type-aware relaxed accuracy not language-aware; different number formatting conventions across languages not discussed; no validation that metric behaves consistently across languages

Shallow fine-tuning insights: Simple LoRA with frozen vision encoders; limited exploration of training strategies; no mechanistic understanding of why fine-tuning helps; comparison with other adaptation methods absent

strengths: Addresses a genuine gap: multilingual chart understanding is largely unexplored and English-centric bias is a documented limitation
Large-scale resource: 154K total images and 777K QA pairs across 10 languages with both test and training splits is substantial
Well-designed construction pipeline: decoupled JSON/code representation enabling multilingual rendering via code reuse is elegant
Rigorous multi-stage quality control: automated validation combined with human verification achieving strong inter-annotator agreement (κ̄w > 0.8)
Comprehensive evaluation coverage: 22 models across general, multilingual, chart-specific, and closed-source categories
Clear empirical findings: quantifies English-language bias, documents sharp performance degradation for low-resource languages, shows consistent fine-tuning gains (20-90%)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: pipeline relies entirely on prior techniques (LLM translation, back-translation, Plotly rendering, LoRA). No methodological innovation justifies top-tier venue publication

Critical LLM dependency undermines reproducibility: entire construction/validation depends on Gemini-2.5-Pro API; future researchers cannot reproduce without access; model behavior may change; circular validation (using model to generate AND validate its own output)

Severe data quality concerns: 65% cumulative filtering (35.9% → 23.2% → 20.5%) suggests pervasive issues; no breakdown by language/chart type; only 20% of test data validated by humans; why such aggressive filtering?
Missing essential baseline: no comparison to simply fine-tuning on machine-translated versions (Google Translate, mT5) of existing datasets; cannot justify LLM-based approach without this comparison

Weak dataset quality validation: even creator model (Gemini-2.5-Pro) achieves only 68.5% accuracy; unclear whether low scores reflect dataset difficulty or quality issues; no calibration against original English datasets

Grossly overclaimed scope: title and abstract claim 'globally inclusive' development supporting '65% of global population' but only cover 10 major languages; missing truly low-resource languages (African, SE Asian); misleadingly label Bengali/Hindi/Arabic/Urdu as 'low-resource' despite 100M+ speakers

Shallow multilingual analysis: Table 4 findings (models preferring English) barely discussed; error categories too generic ('Language Bias' undefined); only 300 errors per model per language examined; no language-specific error patterns identified

Fine-tuning results are confirmatory, not validating: large gains (20-90%) expected from any new dataset; doesn't prove POLYCHARTQA quality is superior or captures meaningful multilingual phenomena; no transfer analysis (do POLYCHARTQA-trained models work on other chart datasets?)
Extensibility problems: LLM-dependent pipeline cannot scale to new languages without proprietary API access; no alternative human-annotation pathway proposed

Inadequate human evaluation: per-language quality breakdown not provided in Table 2; high variance in inter-annotator agreement across languages unexplained (κ̄w 0.657-0.971); only sampling 20% of large test set limits statistical power

strengths: Addresses critical gap: First large-scale multilingual chart QA benchmark spanning 10 languages (22.6K test charts, 751K training examples), filling important blind spot in multilingual LVLM evaluation
Scalable, reproducible pipeline: Clever code/JSON decomposition enables efficient translation without manual re-annotation; comprehensive prompts (Appendix F) ensure reproducibility

Rigorous quality control: Multi-stage validation combining automated checks (visual fidelity, QA validity using dual LLM validators) with human review on 20% subset; strong inter-annotator agreement (κ > 0.88); detailed filtering statistics

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: 22 representative models across 4 categories; clear stratification of performance gaps; cross-lingual analysis revealing model family-specific alignment patterns; fine-tuning improvements 20-93% across diverse architectures

Insightful error analysis: Systematic breakdown of failures (OCR: 27-51%, language bias: 26-61%, reasoning gaps: 9-22%) across error/chart/question types; identifies complex charts (multi-axes, 3D) as major failure sources
Strong practical contribution: Dataset enables immediate applications; fine-tuning results demonstrate value (Qwen2.5-VL-7B reaches Gemini-2.5-Pro parity; weaker models show dramatic improvements)

Excellent presentation and transparency: Clear writing, effective visualizations, extensive appendices with full prompts and statistics; careful source dataset selection justification; honest discussion of limitations
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Pipeline involves straightforward engineering (JSON extraction → LLM translation → rendering); no novel algorithms for multilingual understanding; fine-tuning uses standard LoRA; back-translation validation is standard practice

LLM-dependent quality control: Heavy reliance on proprietary Gemini model for extraction and validation creates potential for systematic bias propagation; difficult to quantify quality ceiling; high filtering rates (23.2% translation, 20.5% visual inspection) suggest possible instability

Incomplete statistical rigor: Results averaged over 8 runs without confidence intervals or significance tests; error analysis based on only 300 samples per model/language; some human evaluation results suspicious (Hindi QA: κ undefined suggesting 100% agreement); no statistical bounds on improvements

Data contamination concerns: Training data sourced from same datasets as test set (ChartQA, ChartLlama, ChartX); potential train-test leakage despite split. Additionally, 'EN' results use regenerated charts rather than original English data, reducing interpretability

Limited language analysis: Only 10 languages despite claims of 'multilingual'; low-resource definition follows prior work without justification; script differences mentioned but not systematically analyzed; no per-language fine-tuning analysis showing which languages benefit most

Shallow experimental analysis: OCR/language bias identified as dominant errors but limited diagnostic insight into addressing them; cross-lingual experiments show expected patterns without deeper investigation; key ablations missing (Why Gemini-2.5-Pro? Why LoRA r=128? Alternative translation strategies?)

Generalization limitations: All evaluation on single chart QA task; generalization to other chart tasks (summarization, generation) unknown; no out-of-domain evaluation; chart type imbalance (bar: 60% in training) may bias fine-tuning

Incomplete baseline comparisons: Recent bilingual work (Chen et al., 2024a; Heakl et al., 2025) mentioned but not directly compared; limited engagement with existing multilingual benchmarks (MTVQA, M3Exam); two-stage fine-tuning adds complexity without clear justification
